statement: In healthy, mostly white adults in their twenties, N-acetylcysteine (NAC) capsules, an over-the-counter supplement, taken during a supervised session of beer drinking, compared with identical dummy capsules taken by the same people in another session, did not detectably change next-morning hangover symptoms in a randomized, double-blind crossover trial of 49 completers (median total symptom score 10 against 13 on a 0 to 52 scale, P = 0.45), nor headache, nausea or weakness separately; comparing women with men, women's scores were lower on NAC than on placebo and men's higher (P = 0.04), a subgroup comparison among several uncorrected tests (Coppersmith et al., 2021). Evidence is insufficient to say whether NAC prevents or eases hangover: only medians were reported, without intervals; one low dose range and one timing were tested; drinking after the session was not controlled; and the difference between women and men needs testing in a trial designed for it. Side effects were few and mild with both NAC and placebo. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one trial, capsules of N-acetylcysteine (NAC), sold as a supplement, did not ease next-morning hangover symptoms compared with dummy capsules. Women seemed to do a little better on NAC and men a little worse, but that may be chance. Side effects were few and mild with both.
population: 49 healthy adults (31 men, 18 women; predominantly white, mostly aged 20 to 30) without alcohol use disorder who completed both sessions, at one US hospital
exposure: N-acetylcysteine capsules at low doses, taken during a supervised session of beer drinking (doses and timing are on the study card)
comparator: Identical lactose placebo capsules taken by the same people during another session with the same drinking target
outcome: Next-morning Hangover Symptoms Scale total score; headache, nausea and weakness; side effects
magnitude: Medians, no intervals: total score 10 against 13 (P = 0.45; 19% against 25% of the maximum); headache 1 against 1 (P = 0.93); nausea 0 against 1 (P = 0.11); weakness 1 against 1 (P = 0.72); five-item subset 5 against 5.5 (P = 0.86). Difference scores by sex (NAC minus placebo): women −3.5, men +2 (P = 0.04); nausea P = 0.05, weakness P = 0.03, headache P = 0.32. Side effects after NAC: gastrointestinal 4, headache 2, rash 1, muscle twitches 1, insomnia 1; after placebo: headache 3, gastrointestinal 1.

evidence.extracted: Primary outcome: total Hangover Symptoms Scale score did not differ significantly between NAC and placebo (median 10 against 13, P = 0.45; 19% against 25% of the maximum); headache (1 against 1, P = 0.93), nausea (0 against 1, P = 0.11) and weakness (1 against 1, P = 0.72) did not differ significantly either.

A subset of five valid items gave the same result: median 5 (range 0 to 19) with NAC against 5.5 (0 to 20) with placebo, P = 0.86 (analysed as independent groups with Mann-Whitney tests; 91 observations against 98 expected from 49 completers in two sessions, editors' calculation).

evidence.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 legend; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
evidence.extracted: Difference scores (NAC minus placebo) were −3.5 in women and +2 in men (P = 0.04), with sex differences for nausea (P = 0.05) and weakness (P = 0.03) but not headache (P = 0.32); the Discussion calls the symptom comparisons post hoc.

Side effects attributed to the pill: after NAC, gastrointestinal symptoms (4), headache (2), rash (1), muscle twitches (1) and insomnia (1); after placebo, headache (3) and gastrointestinal symptoms (1); no serious adverse events.

62 enrolled and 49 completed. The authors name as limitations the low doses, supervised sessions that ended at a breath alcohol target and may have produced milder hangovers than unrestricted drinking, possible drinking after leaving, and unsupervised completion of the scale at home.

risk_of_bias.note: Well blinded and randomized, but 21% of those enrolled were lost and only completers analysed, the interval between sessions is unreported, drinking after the session was uncontrolled, and analyses beyond the primary outcome are inconsistently described.

indirectness.note: Low doses at one timing during supervised drinking to a fixed target, unlike most real drinking occasions.

imprecision.note: Medians without intervals in 49 people; ranges are wide and a moderate effect cannot be excluded.

grade.reasoning: A randomized, double-blind crossover trial starts high; downgraded for risk of bias, indirectness and twice for imprecision, giving very low. The relation is insufficient evidence because no interval excludes a meaningful effect. The benefit in women is not part of the claim's finding: it is a subgroup difference among several uncorrected tests, with men scoring worse on NAC. The published correction changes only an Introduction passage and does not affect these results. Single study.
